clue.text: Dictator broken by dismissal, rub salt in wound

indicators.note: a word broken by another is split open so the second sits in the gap

blocks.note: Vladimir Putin, the Russian leader, often called a dictator
getting the boot is being sacked

explanation.surface: A tyrant, ousted from power, makes his humiliation even worse.
explanation.walkthrough: PUT...IN opens up to take THE BOOT, giving PUT THE BOOT IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe deliberately making someone's suffering worse once they are already down.

clue.text: Issue hurdling boat in discipline with obstacles

indicators.note: to hurdle something is to stretch over it, so the first word straddles the second

blocks.note: to issue is to flow out or pour
Noah's ark is a boat

explanation.surface: A problem arises when someone tries jumping a boat during an obstacle sport.
explanation.walkthrough: P-OUR straddles ARK: P(ARK)OUR. 'Hurdling' fits the athletic surface but here means sitting either side of.
explanation.definitionFit: Parkour is the urban sport of running, vaulting and climbing across walls, rails and other physical barriers.

clue.text: Dead round

blocks.note: first meaning: finished, doomed
second meaning: a drink raised to someone, as one round of salutes at a dinner

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated words that each mean the same short answer; 'round' is a toast proposed at a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses the word for someone doomed, and it also names a ceremonial raising of glasses in honour of somebody.

clue.text: Old money has Ivy League member in clover, say

indicators.note: the second word has the first, holding it inside itself

blocks.note: clover is one crop cut and dried for fodder; 'say' marks it as an example
the University of Pennsylvania, known as Penn, is in the Ivy League

explanation.surface: Old-school wealth: an elite American student living in clover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In clover' looks like the idiom for living well, but clover is the HAY that holds PENN: HA(PENN)Y.
explanation.definitionFit: The halfpenny was a pre-decimal British coin, worth half a penny, withdrawn from circulation in 1969 and later revived briefly.

clue.text: Peer offering testament on seafood, shortly

indicators.note: made short, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a squid is eaten as seafood (calamari)
NT is the New Testament

explanation.surface: A lord presents a will about a fish supper, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a noble, but it is the verb: to look narrowly. SQUI(d) comes first, with NT put on it.
explanation.definitionFit: To squint is to look with eyes half closed, which is what peering at something hard involves.

clue.text: One not drinking alcohol, tiniest amount of Cinzano spat out by duck?

indicators.note: something spat out is expelled, so that letter is removed from the word

blocks.note: the first letter, the smallest bit of the drink
a duck is a quacker, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A duck takes a sip of Cinzano, an Italian vermouth, and spits it out like a teetotaller.
explanation.walkthrough: C is removed from QUACKER. Quakers have a long tradition of abstaining from alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Religious Society of Friends traditionally abstain from strong drink as part of their testimony of simplicity.

clue.text: Very soon plague carrier brought a flame

blocks.note: 'in a mo' is informal for in a moment
rats carried the fleas that spread bubonic plague
taken as written

explanation.surface: Any moment now a rodent will bring a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flame' sounds like fire after 'plague', but an old flame is a sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: An inamorata is a female lover, and 'flame' is a common term for a romantic partner, especially a past one.

clue.text: Play with leading character in turmoil, case of denial in general

indicators.note: the leading character of a word is its opening letter
the case of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters
one piece goes inside the next word, which then encloses it

blocks.note: the opening letter of turmoil
general, as in widespread, is wide
the outside letters of denial

explanation.surface: A leader in chaos fiddles while broadly refusing to admit anything.
explanation.walkthrough: T then WI(DL)DE. 'General' is the adjective meaning broad, not an army rank.
explanation.definitionFit: To twiddle is to fiddle idly with something, turning it about with the fingers, which is playing with it.

clue.text: Spectacular drop as champion hits the canvas, Ali’s arms held up

indicators.note: the arms of a word stick out at each side, so its two end letters
in a down clue, holding something up means reading it bottom to top

blocks.note: a victor is a winner
the end letters of Ali, flipped to IA
a boxer who hits the canvas falls to the floor of the ring

explanation.surface: A boxing scene: the winner goes down while Muhammad Ali raises his arms in triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: VICTOR, then IA, then FALLS. Muhammad Ali is the famous boxer.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria Falls, on the Zambezi between Zambia and Zimbabwe, is one of the world's largest and most dramatic waterfalls.

clue.text: Sea monster finishing off Balearic islands?

indicators.note: only the finishing part is kept, with the front of the name dropped

blocks.note: Majorca or Minorca, two Balearic islands; the question mark allows either

explanation.surface: A question about some legendary beast lurking off the Spanish islands.
explanation.walkthrough: Majorca and Minorca share the same ending, which is why 'islands' is plural: both finish ORCA.
explanation.definitionFit: The orca, or killer whale, is a huge ocean predator, loosely described as a monster of the deep.

clue.text: Pressure on America if a shambles, to all appearances

indicators.note: a shambles is a complete mess, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure
the letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: Political commentary: pressure would mount on the USA if things fell apart, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: Prima facie is Latin for 'at first sight', meaning on the face of things or as it seems.

clue.text: See 1
See 22
Will claims Dick works near building site?

indicators.note: to claim is to take hold of, so the first word holds the second

blocks.note: Will Shakespeare is the Bard
Dick and Ricky are both pet forms of Richard

explanation.surface: A will names a man called Dick as heir to some factory near a construction site.
explanation.walkthrough: B(RICKY)ARD. 'Will' looks like a legal document, but it is Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickyard is a works where bricks are made, the sort of place that supplies building projects nearby.

clue.text: Ridge in black rock for insect

indicators.note: one word goes in the other, enclosed by it

blocks.note: coal is a black rock
a chine is a ridge, as of a hill or a backbone

explanation.surface: A dark crag with a ridge is home to some bug.
explanation.walkthrough: CO(CHINE)AL. 'Black' and 'rock' work together as one thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cochineal is a scale bug from Mexico, crushed to make a red food dye; the name covers both creature and colouring.

clue.text: See 21
Deal stuffed, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: the sound, not the spelling, is what counts here

blocks.note: stuffed full is packed

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether an agreement was stitched up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal agreement or treaty between parties, which is a deal.

clue.text: Used up, looking at new token for beer

indicators.note: in a down clue, using the letters upwards means reading them bottom to top

blocks.note: re means concerning or regarding
N is short for new
a slip of paper can serve as a token or voucher

explanation.surface: Someone has spent their voucher and is eyeing a fresh one for a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used up' reads like 'exhausted', but it tells you to write the whole string upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilsner is a pale, crisp lager first brewed in the Czech city of Plzen, a style of beer.

clue.text: Good to see message about humanity originally attributed to monastery

indicators.note: originally points at the start, so only the opening letter
about means around, so the message wraps the letter

blocks.note: a wat is a Buddhist monastery or temple in Thailand
a cable is a telegram
the opening letter of humanity

explanation.surface: A monastery is credited with a pleasing message about the human race.
explanation.walkthrough: WAT then C(H)ABLE. A wat is the Thai word for a temple complex.
explanation.definitionFit: Something watchable is worth viewing, fit to be enjoyed by an audience, as with a decent television programme.

clue.text: Grant that’s secured absolutely not for the French clergy

indicators.note: something secured is held fast, so the name grips the other word

blocks.note: Cary Grant, the Hollywood actor
French for no

explanation.surface: A grant has been secured, but the French clergy are flatly refused.
explanation.walkthrough: CA(NON)RY. 'Grant' looks like an award of money, but it is a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A canonry is the post of a canon, and by extension the canons of a cathedral as a body of churchmen.

clue.text: Beastly and brave rule on ineffective banks

indicators.note: the run of words banks, or holds within its sides, a word inside

blocks.note: spanning the end of rule, all of on, and the start of ineffective

explanation.surface: A savage, courageous ruling against useless financial institutions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like money, but it says the words hold the answer: ru(LE ON INE)ffective.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonine means lion-like: the lion is a beast and a byword for courage, so both words fit.

clue.text: Squat where food processor stored by operative

indicators.note: stored means kept inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: a secret operative is a spy
the stomach, or tum, processes food

explanation.surface: An agent hides a kitchen gadget in some derelict building.
explanation.walkthrough: S(TUM)PY. 'Food processor' is the kitchen gadget on the surface, the belly underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Squat as an adjective means short and thick-set, which is what stumpy describes.

clue.text: Party leader has admitted tellin’ stories to lose the plot

indicators.note: admitting someone lets them in, so the name takes the phrase inside

blocks.note: Nigel Farage, leader of the British party Reform UK
telling stories is lying, with the dropped g kept

explanation.surface: A politician confesses to fibbing to people and then losing control.
explanation.walkthrough: F(LYIN' TO)ARAGE. Nigel Farage is a well-known British right-wing politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing the plot is a British idiom for losing self-control, flaring into sudden anger or irrational behaviour.

clue.text: Particular area, part of body doctor showed: foot

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are altered in order

blocks.note: the neck is part of the body
the letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A medic examines a patient: which bit hurts? The foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a medic beside 'part of body', but it is a verb meaning tamper.
explanation.definitionFit: Your neck of the woods is an idiom for your local district or the region where someone lives.

clue.text: Afford to listen to island?

indicators.note: listening means the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: said out, Afford is 'a Ford'

explanation.surface: Can you afford a trip to an island? Listen and decide.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ford Capri was a popular 1970s coupe; the Italian island shares its name, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is a rocky island in the Bay of Naples, famous as a holiday resort.

clue.text: Having curbed expression, 1-0 ahead of an Italian team

indicators.note: curbing restrains, so the score holds the word inside it

blocks.note: one-nil: I is one, NIL is nothing
a term is a word or expression
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football report: a 1-0 lead with no celebrating, before facing an Italian side.
explanation.walkthrough: I + N(TERM)IL + AN. The 1-0 scoreline is read as I and NIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Inter Milan, properly Internazionale, is a major Italian football club based in Milan.

clue.text: Bluenose Republican in scumbag

indicators.note: one letter goes in the other word, enclosed by it

blocks.note: pig is an insult for a nasty person
R stands for Republican

explanation.surface: A puritanical American politician is exposed as a sleaze.
explanation.walkthrough: P(R)IG. A bluenose is a puritanical, disapproving person.
explanation.definitionFit: A prig is a smugly self-righteous person, and bluenose is a mainly American term for a prudish moraliser.

clue.text: Sun features European article in reports

indicators.note: something that features a thing includes it, so these hold the article

blocks.note: the sun's rays, what the sun gives off
el is the Spanish word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A tabloid newspaper prints a European piece among its stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' looks like the British tabloid, but it is the star giving off light: R(EL)AYS.
explanation.definitionFit: To relay is to pass on information, so relays and reports are both verbs for communicating news.

clue.text: Credit given to journalist via bank

blocks.note: via means by way of
a bank, as of switches or oars, is a row or line

explanation.surface: A reporter receives payment through a financial institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credit' and 'bank' suggest money; the credit is the name printed on a story.
explanation.definitionFit: A byline is the line naming the writer at the top of a newspaper article, acknowledging authorship.
